summary.title: Test-driven development - Wikipedia
summary.one_liner: Test-driven development (TDD) is a red-green-refactor workflow where you write a failing automated test first, write just enough code to pass it, then refactor, and this article explains its steps, practices, anti-patterns, and the evidence on its benefits.
takeaways: TDD cycle: list scenarios, write a failing test, write the simplest passing code, then refactor while keeping tests green, and repeat.
Tests are written first so the developer considers requirements and interface design before implementing.
Keep unit tests small and fast, use test doubles for external dependencies, and add integration tests separately.
Avoid anti-patterns such as dependent tests, testing implementation details, and slow tests.
Empirical results are mixed: quality gains are more consistent than productivity gains, and TDD does not replace other testing.
summary.summary: The Wikipedia article defines test-driven development as a repeated cycle of writing an automated unit test that fails, writing minimal code to pass it, and refactoring both test and production code. It covers the history (credited to Kent Beck and xUnit), a six-step coding cycle, development style principles such as YAGNI and "fake it till you make it", and best practices for test structure (setup, execution, validation, cleanup) and anti-patterns. It also compares TDD with ATDD and BDD, lists xUnit and TAP tooling, and summarizes meta-analyses on quality and productivity, along with the limits and maintenance costs of TDD.
